newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Brazil posts lowest inflation since 1950.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Brazil posts lowest inflation since 1950.

text.p: Brazil posted its lowest annual inflation rate in almost 50 years last year and should wrestle price increases down to single digits in 1997, economists said.
The closely watched Fipe consumer price index, released on Wednesday by the Economic Research Institute, rose just 10.03 percent in 1996, the lowest increase in the benchmark index since 1950.

"Inflation came in a lot lower than we thought it would. At the beginning of the year, most people were talking about 15 percent or 13 percent," said Thomas Souza, an economist at Merrill Lynch in Brazil.

Stable industrial costs and a continued opening of the Brazilian economy to imports -- which forced local producers to keep prices down -- were seen as the main reasons for the better-than-expected number.
Although the Fipe index only tracks prices in the greater Sao Paulo area, it is one of Brazil's most respected inflation indicators.

Another closely watched indicator, the Getulio Vargas Foundation's IGP-M index, posted 1996 inflation of 9.20 percent, against 15.25 percent the year before. In addition to consumer prices, however, the IGP-M index measures wholesale and construction costs in Rio de Janeiro and Sao Paulo.

The favorable 1996 results come 30 months into the government's economic stabilization drive, known as the Real Plan, which has slashed inflation through a mix of tight monetary policy and a strong currency.
Brazilian consumer inflation as measured by Fipe fell from nearly 2,500 percent in 1993 to just 23 percent in 1995, the first full year of the Real Plan.
And economists say the trend toward lower inflation should continue next year.

"There are two main things that will keep inflation down next year: one is falling agricultural prices and the other is smaller adjustments in public utilities," said an economist at a leading U.S. bank in Brazil who requested anonymity.
He noted that prices for soybeans and other Brazilian agricultural products should remain flat in 1997 and that public utility rates should rise about eight percent, compared to 10 percent last year.

Barring any surprises, consumer prices are expected to rise by between six percent and eight percent in 1997. Wholesale price inflation, which rose about eight percent in 1996, could fall to five percent this year, economists said.
"And there will be room for more declines in 1998," Merrill Lynch's Souza said, forecasting consumer price inflation of between five percent and six percent in 1998.
